Theme

Body, health & movement · Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

suffer verb

from an illness or pain

also suffer from, be suffering from, be in pain, have (an illness), suffering

classical

Cic. Fam. 7.26.1: graviter ex intestīnīs labōrārem
Cic. Fam. 9.23: ex pedibus labōrārēs
Traupman 56, 64, 387

labōrō, labōrāre, labōrāvī, labōrātum

verb, first conjugation: with ex and the ablative of the part, or the ablative of the illness

suffer from, be troubled by

Properly “toil, be in difficulty”. Of the part that hurts, ex: ex pedibus, ex rēnibus (Cic. Tusc. 2.60, Lewis & Short); of the illness, the ablative: gravēdine labōrāre, to have a cold (Traupman 56, 63).

Other words

  • afficior, afficī, affectus sum — be suffering (from), be afflicted with

    the passive of afficiō, with the ablative · also used · classical · Cic. Fam. 6.19: dolōribus pedum (Lewis & Short, s.v. afficiō); Traupman 64

    dolōre afficī, to be in pain (Traupman 105, 152); morbō affectus, ill.

  • doleō, dolēre, doluī, dolitum — be in pain, hurt

    verb, second conjugation · also used · classical · Cic. Tusc. 2.35: cum varicēs secābantur C. Mariō, dolēbat

    See hurt. Cicero keeps the two verbs apart: aliud est dolēre, aliud labōrāre: Marius felt pain when his varicose veins were cut, and toiled when he led the march in great heat (Tusc. 2.35); there labōrāre is toil, not illness.

Examples

  • Cum decimum jam diem graviter ex intestīnīs labōrārem

    When I had been suffering badly with my stomach for ten days nowCic. Fam. 7.26.1

  • dīxit tē in lectō esse, quod ex pedibus labōrārēs

    he told me you were in bed because you were suffering with your feetCic. Fam. 9.23

  • Gravēdine labōrās.

    You’ve got a cold (literally, you are suffering from a cold).Traupman 56

See also ill, hurt, disease, suffer.
